chapters.title: Choose the property that differs between components
chapters.formula: Separation: exploit a property difference; analysis: identify or measure composition
chapters.script: Welcome to Purification and Analysis. This recorded Chemistry class uses an AI generated Marin voice. Purification separates a desired substance from impurities by exploiting differences in properties. It does not normally change the desired compound into a new chemical. A mixture of an insoluble solid and a solution may be filtered, but filtering a dissolved impurity does not remove it merely because its particles are invisible. Qualitative analysis asks which elements or groups are present; quantitative analysis measures how much. Characterisation may combine composition with physical or chemical behaviour. A sharp melting range can support purity for a suitable solid, but one measurement alone does not prove identity or perfect purity under every circumstance. Consider sand mixed with a dissolved salt solution. Filtering can retain the sand while the salt remains in the filtrate. Recovering that dissolved salt requires another principle, such as removing solvent or crystallizing under suitable conditions. The proposed method should identify which component is retained, which moves to another phase and whether the desired compound's chemical identity is preserved.
points: Suspended insoluble solid · Filtration · Dissolved solute passes
Dissolved desired solid · Crystallization · Depends on solubility
Identity question · Combined evidence · One property is not proof

chapters.title: Crystallization uses temperature-dependent solubility
chapters.formula: Recrystallization needs a useful difference between hot and cold solubility
chapters.script: A suitable recrystallization solvent dissolves much of the desired solid when hot and less when cold, allowing crystals to form on cooling. Impurities may remain in solution or be removed as insoluble material at a suitable stage. The choice must avoid unwanted chemical reaction with the compound. Cooling does not force every last molecule into crystals; some desired product remains dissolved, so yield and purity are different goals. If the solvent dissolves the product equally well hot and cold, simple cooling is less useful. Sublimation instead exploits a solid's ability to enter the vapour phase and redeposit, separating it from suitably nonvolatile impurities. Suppose a stated solvent quantity dissolves ten grams of a compound when hot but only two grams at the final cold temperature. Starting from a hot saturated solution, at most eight grams could crystallize in that simplified model before additional losses. A larger recovered mass is not automatically purer material. Solubility data, solvent quantity and final temperature are necessary before calculating a theoretical recovery.
points: Hot saturation · 10 g · Starting amount
Cold equilibrium · 2 g · Remains dissolved
Ideal recovery · 10 − 2 · 8 g crystals maximum

chapters.title: Distillation uses vapour composition
chapters.formula: Boiling occurs when total vapour pressure matches external pressure
chapters.script: Distillation vaporizes part of a liquid mixture and condenses the vapour. A more volatile component is often enriched in that vapour. Simple distillation suits some widely separated boiling behaviour or removal of a volatile liquid from nonvolatile material; closer boiling liquids may require fractional distillation with repeated vapour-liquid contact. Reduced-pressure distillation lowers the boiling temperature and can help avoid thermal decomposition. Steam distillation applies to suitable water-immiscible, steam-volatile compounds because their vapour pressures contribute to the total. No method guarantees separation of every mixture: azeotropes and chemical instability can limit ordinary distillation. Boiling occurs when the relevant vapour pressure reaches the external pressure. Lowering external pressure can therefore reduce the required temperature. A fractionating column provides repeated separation opportunities rather than acting as a chemical reagent. Choose the method from volatility, thermal stability and mixture behaviour, and recognize when an azeotrope prevents the assumed unlimited enrichment by ordinary fractional distillation.
points: Fractional · Closer volatility · Azeotropes possible
Reduced pressure · Lower boiling temperature · Stability still matters
Steam · Suitable immiscible compound · Not every liquid

chapters.title: Extraction and chromatography redistribute a substance
chapters.formula: R_f = spot travel distance / solvent-front travel distance
chapters.script: Differential extraction distributes a solute between suitable immiscible solvents. The amount in each phase depends on its affinity and the phase volumes; repeated smaller extractions can be more effective than one extraction of the same total solvent volume under an appropriate partition model. Do not assume every organic substance must prefer the organic phase. Chromatography separates components because they interact differently with stationary and mobile phases. In elementary paper or thin-layer work, R f is the distance travelled by the spot divided by the distance travelled by the solvent front from the same starting line. It depends on the system and conditions, so matching one R f alone does not prove identity. If a chromatographic spot travels three centimetres and the solvent front five centimetres from the same origin, the ratio is zero point six. Both distances use the same length units. Those units cancel, so the ratio is dimensionless. A new solvent or stationary phase can change the value for the same compound. In extraction, always state which phase is being analysed and include the phase volumes when translating a concentration ratio into recovered amounts.
points: Spot · 3 cm · Same origin
Solvent front · 5 cm · Same system
Rf · 3 / 5 = 0.60 · Dimensionless

chapters.title: Element detection converts a hidden element into a detectable form
chapters.formula: Qualitative observation requires the correct conversion and control of interfering species
chapters.script: In organic compounds an element can be covalently bound and not respond directly as a free ion. Classical sodium-fusion analysis converts suitable nitrogen, sulfur or halogen content into ionic products that can be tested. The chemistry involves reactive metal and hazardous products and belongs only in a supervised laboratory, not an improvised home experiment. Nitrogen can be detected through cyanide-derived iron-complex chemistry, sulfur through sulfide chemistry and halogens through suitable silver-halide precipitation after removing interferences. Simultaneous nitrogen and sulfur can form thiocyanate, altering the expected observations. Phosphorus detection can involve oxidation to phosphate followed by a suitable phosphate test. A negative poorly performed test is not proof an element is absent. Classical element tests first transform covalently bound elements into species with recognizable reactions. This explains why directly adding an ionic test reagent to an untreated organic compound may fail. A positive observation needs the expected chemistry and interference controls; a negative observation also depends on successful conversion and detection. Treat the test result as evidence within a stated analytical scheme rather than an infallible label.
points: Nitrogen · Ionic detectable species · Conversion must succeed
Sulfur / halogen · Suitable ionic products · Remove interference
Negative test · No observed response · Not absolute proof

board.heading: Element detection converts a hidden element into a detectable form

chapters.title: Combustion data count carbon and hydrogen
chapters.script: Complete combustion analysis can relate collected products to carbon and hydrogen in a sample. Carbon is measured through carbon dioxide, while hydrogen is measured through water. With carbon atomic mass twelve and oxygen sixteen, carbon accounts for twelve forty fourths of the carbon dioxide mass. With hydrogen one, hydrogen accounts for two eighteenths of water mass. Convert product masses to element masses before dividing by sample mass to obtain percentages. Only assign the remaining mass to oxygen when the problem establishes that no other unmeasured element or impurity contributes. A zero point three zero zero gram sample gives zero point four four zero gram carbon dioxide and zero point one eight zero gram water. These correspond to zero point one two zero gram carbon and zero point zero two zero gram hydrogen. Under the stated carbon hydrogen oxygen assumption, oxygen mass is zero point one six zero gram. The masses add back to the sample mass. The carbon percentage is forty and the hydrogen percentage about six point six seven. Product mass can exceed sample mass because oxygen from combustion also enters those products.
points: O by difference · 0.160 g O · Only C, H, O assumed

chapters.title: Other elemental estimates need their own chemical assumptions
chapters.formula: Element mass from a pure weighed precipitate = precipitate mass x element molar-mass fraction
chapters.script: Dumas nitrogen estimation measures nitrogen gas after suitable conversion and removal of interfering gases. The measured gas volume needs stated temperature, pressure and appropriate corrections. Kjeldahl analysis estimates nitrogen through conversion to ammonium and subsequent ammonia measurement, but does not work without modification for every nitrogen-containing functional group. Classical Carius-type halogen estimation converts suitable halogen content to a weighed silver halide; the halogen fraction follows its molar-mass share in that precipitate. Sulfur can similarly be estimated through sulfate precipitation, and phosphorus through an appropriate phosphate-derived measurement. These are stoichiometric principles, not instructions for hazardous digestion or pressure-vessel operation. For nitrogen gas collected over water, the pressure of water vapour must be considered before applying the gas law to dry nitrogen. For a weighed silver halide, the halogen amount follows a molar mass fraction rather than equality with the whole precipitate mass. Each method has its own conversion chemistry, so a calculation valid for carbon dioxide cannot simply be reused for every analytical product.
points: Dumas · Nitrogen gas · P, V, T; water vapour
Silver halide · Precipitate mass · Halogen mass fraction
Kjeldahl · Ammonia-related amount · Functional-group limits

board.heading: Other elemental estimates need their own chemical assumptions

chapters.title: An empirical ratio is not yet a molecular formula
chapters.formula: Molecular formula = empirical formula subscripts x (molar mass / empirical-formula mass)
chapters.script: Convert each element mass or percentage to moles using its atomic mass, then divide all amounts by the smallest. Find a simple integer ratio without rounding a genuine fraction away: a ratio near one to one and a half may need multiplication by two. The empirical formula describes the simplest atom ratio. To find a molecular formula, divide the independently known molar mass by the empirical-formula mass. A suitable result is an integer multiplier, within the precision of the data. Multiplying every empirical subscript gives the molecular formula; it still does not uniquely identify structure. Report assumptions and rounding rather than forcing inconsistent data into a familiar compound. An empirical unit with one carbon, two hydrogens and one oxygen has approximate formula mass thirty using the stated rounded atomic masses. If independent molar mass is ninety, the multiplier is three, giving three carbons, six hydrogens and three oxygens. Multiplying only one subscript would change the elemental ratio and fail the original analysis. Molecular formula still leaves possible structural isomers.
points: Empirical unit · 12 + 2 + 16 · 30
Molar mass ratio · 90 / 30 · 3
Molecular formula · Multiply every subscript · C₃H₆O₃

chapters.title: Correct nitrogen gas for water vapour
chapters.formula: Pdry = Ptotal − Pwater; n(N₂) = PdryV/(RT)
chapters.script: Dumas style nitrogen analysis requires the amount of dry nitrogen gas, not an uncorrected wet gas volume at an assumed standard condition. Suppose supplied results for a zero point two five zero gram suitable sample give twenty point zero millilitres nitrogen collected over water at three hundred kelvin. Total pressure is one hundred kilopascals and the supplied water vapour pressure is three point zero zero kilopascals. The nitrogen partial pressure is therefore ninety seven point zero kilopascals. Convert the volume to zero point zero two zero zero litre and use R eight point three one four litre kilopascal per mole kelvin. The ideal gas calculation gives about zero point zero zero zero seven seven seven eight mole nitrogen molecules. Each molecule contains two nitrogen atoms, so the nitrogen mass uses molar mass twenty eight grams per mole of gas, giving about zero point zero two one eight gram. Relative to the sample, nitrogen is about eight point seven one percent. Assume quantitative conversion and gas collection with no other gases present after the stated analytical treatment. If the gas is already dry, do not subtract water pressure again. Temperature, pressure units and the two nitrogen atoms per molecule must all be handled explicitly.

chapters.title: Back titration counts captured ammonia
chapters.formula: n(NH₃) = initial acid equivalents − residual acid equivalents
chapters.script: A Kjeldahl style numerical problem counts ammonia formed from nitrogen that the stated method converts quantitatively. Use supplied results for a zero point five zero zero gram suitable sample. Its ammonia is captured by twenty five point zero millilitres of zero point one zero zero molar hydrochloric acid. The remaining acid requires ten point zero millilitres of zero point one zero zero molar sodium hydroxide. Initial acid amount is two point five zero millimoles and the residual amount one point zero zero millimole. The difference, one point five zero millimoles, equals captured ammonia and therefore nitrogen atom amount in this model. Multiplying by fourteen gives zero point zero two one zero gram nitrogen, or four point two zero percent of the original sample. Using all the initial acid would overestimate nitrogen. The standard textbook method is not generally applicable to nitrogen in nitro or azo groups or pyridine type rings without appropriate modification; quantitative conversion cannot be assumed for every nitrogen compound. These are interpretation and stoichiometry steps for supplied analytical data, not a procedure for carrying out hazardous digestion or handling laboratory reagents.

chapters.title: Convert a silver-halide mass to halogen mass
chapters.formula: One mole AgCl contains one mole Cl atoms
chapters.script: Gravimetric halogen analysis measures a compound containing the halogen, not a pure mass of the halogen itself. Suppose a supplied halogen analysis result says zero point two zero zero gram of a suitable chlorine containing organic sample yields zero point one four three five gram silver chloride. Assume the collected solid is pure dry silver chloride and the conversion and recovery are quantitative. With supplied molar masses one hundred forty three point five for silver chloride and thirty five point five for chlorine, the precipitate amount is zero point zero zero one zero zero mole. Each formula unit contains one chlorine, so chlorine mass is zero point zero three five five gram. The sample chlorine percentage is seventeen point seven five. Do not treat the entire silver chloride mass as chlorine or divide by chlorine gas molar mass seventy one when counting individual chlorine atoms in the salt. Different halogens require the corresponding silver halide molar mass, and mixed precipitates need additional information. Contamination, light induced changes or incomplete recovery can invalidate the simple mass conversion. This chapter uses reported results and chemical accounting; it does not provide a sealed tube experimental recipe.

chapters.title: Compare one extraction with repeated portions
chapters.formula: Fraction left in water = Vaq/(Vaq + K Vorg) in the stated partition model
chapters.script: Repeated solvent portions can remove more solute than one extraction using the same total solvent volume. Consider a neutral solute with constant partition ratio K equal to organic concentration divided by aqueous concentration, taking value four. Assume two immiscible phases with unchanged volumes, complete equilibration, no reaction or ionization and negligible mutual solubility. Begin with one hundred millilitres aqueous phase. A single fresh twenty five millilitre organic portion leaves aqueous fraction one hundred divided by one hundred plus four times twenty five, or one half. Now use two fresh twelve point five millilitre portions in sequence, separating each organic portion before the next contact. Each leaves fraction one hundred divided by one hundred plus fifty, or two thirds, of the solute then present in water. After both, the remaining fraction is four ninths, so about fifty five point six percent has been extracted rather than fifty percent. The second contact acts on the remainder, not the original amount. This calculation assumes a fixed partition ratio for the specified chemical form; changing p H or allowing association can require a more complete distribution model.

Each of two 12.5 mL portions · 100/(100 + 4×12.5) · 2/3 of current amount remains

chapters.title: Chromatographic agreement is evidence not identity
chapters.formula: Rf = solute travel / solvent-front travel for the same run
chapters.script: Chromatography compares movement under specified stationary phase, mobile phase and experimental conditions. Suppose the solvent front travels five point zero zero centimetres while two sample spots travel two point zero zero and three point five zero centimetres from the same origin. Their retention factors are zero point four zero and zero point seven zero. Both ratios are dimensionless and use the solvent front distance rather than the plate height or the distance between spots. A reference substance with retention factor zero point four zero under the same conditions supports a possible assignment of the first spot, but matching one value does not uniquely prove chemical identity. Different compounds can migrate together, and an apparently single spot does not guarantee absolute purity. Changing solvent composition or using another suitable analytical method can supply independent evidence. When calculating recovery, compare recovered analyte mass with the amount originally present; the mass of an isolated fraction can include solvent or impurities. Keep separation, recovery and identification as distinct claims. Record the run conditions and the observed number of resolved components rather than treating a familiar retention factor as an invariant molecular constant.
points: Second spot 3.50 cm · 3.50 / 5.00 · Rf = 0.70
Matching a reference Rf · Same conditions required · Supporting evidence, not proof

chapters.title: Sulfur gravimetry counts the sulfur in a weighed product
chapters.formula: Pure BaSO₄ contains one sulfur per formula unit
chapters.script: Gravimetric elemental analysis converts an element into a product of known composition and measures that product mass. In a supplied quantitative sulfur model, all sample sulfur is recovered in pure dry barium sulfate. Use molar masses barium sulfate two hundred thirty three and sulfur thirty two grams per mole. A zero point two zero zero gram sample gives zero point two three three gram barium sulfate. Product amount is zero point zero zero one zero zero mole, and each formula unit contains one sulfur atom, so the sulfur amount is the same. Sulfur mass is zero point zero three two zero gram, giving sixteen percent of the original sample mass. Do not assign the entire precipitate mass to sulfur; most of it is barium and oxygen. The calculation assumes complete conversion, quantitative collection and the specified dry product. Retained moisture or unrelated coprecipitated material would bias an actual mass, while incomplete collection could lower recovery. These supplied-data assumptions connect an observation to a composition calculation. They are not an experimental oxidation or precipitation procedure.

chapters.title: Phosphorus gravimetry needs the factor of two
chapters.formula: Mg₂P₂O₇ contains two phosphorus atoms per formula unit
chapters.script: A gravimetric product can contain more than one atom of the element being estimated. In a supplied phosphorus analysis model, all sample phosphorus is recovered as pure dry magnesium pyrophosphate. Its formula contains two magnesium, two phosphorus and seven oxygen atoms. Use supplied molar mass two hundred twenty two grams per mole and phosphorus atomic mass thirty one. Suppose a zero point three one zero gram sample gives zero point two two two gram of the specified product. That is zero point zero zero one zero zero mole product, containing zero point zero zero two zero zero mole phosphorus atoms. Phosphorus mass is zero point zero six two zero gram and its sample mass percentage is twenty. Using one phosphorus atom per product unit would halve the answer incorrectly. Likewise, a different weighed form would require its own formula factor rather than reuse this conversion unchanged. Quantitative recovery and a defined dry product are assumptions, and this numerical model does not supply hazardous sample-conversion steps. Start from the product formula and the counted atom before writing a shortcut percentage expression.

chapters.title: Oxygen by difference needs a complete mass basis
chapters.formula: O% = 100 − sum(other measured mass percentages), only when the remainder is oxygen
chapters.script: An elemental percentage obtained by difference is conditional on what the remainder can contain. Suppose a dry sample contains only carbon, hydrogen, nitrogen, sulfur and oxygen. Supplied measured mass percentages are sixty, eight, twelve and four for the first four elements respectively. They sum to eighty four, leaving sixteen percent oxygen under the stated complete composition model. A half gram sample would then contain zero point zero eight zero gram oxygen. Unmeasured halogens, inorganic residue or retained water would make the same subtraction an unreliable oxygen determination unless separately accounted for. All percentages must also refer to the same sample basis; mixing dry basis carbon with a wet basis sample mass breaks the balance. Difference calculations combine measurement uncertainty. If the four supplied small worst case bounds are zero point three, zero point one, zero point two and zero point one percentage points, their conservative sum is zero point seven percentage points for the inferred oxygen fraction. This is not automatically a statistical standard deviation. State the composition model, sample basis and uncertainty interpretation along with the remainder.

chapters.title: Steam-distillation mole and mass ratios are different
chapters.formula: Ideal immiscible phases present: nA/nwater = pA°/pwater°
chapters.script: Steam distillation of a suitable immiscible pair uses the vapour pressures contributed by both liquid phases at the same temperature. In an idealized supplied example, the organic component contributes ten kilopascals and water ninety. Their sum is one hundred kilopascals, so the mixture can boil against that external pressure while both liquid phases remain present. The vapour organic mole fraction is one tenth. The mole ratio of organic vapour to water vapour is one to nine. A mass ratio also needs molar masses. With organic molar mass one hundred eighty and water eighteen grams per mole, organic mass divided by water mass is ten times one hundred eighty divided by ninety times eighteen, or ten ninths. Thus a representative condensed fraction containing ten grams water would contain about eleven point one grams organic component under this model. Applying liquid mole fractions as though the liquids formed one ideal miscible solution would describe a different model. Phase exhaustion, appreciable mutual solubility, entrainment or chemical instability can invalidate the simple ratio. Keep phase presence, vapour composition and condensed mass accounting explicit.

chapters.title: Silver precipitation needs interference control
chapters.formula: Ag⁺ + Cl⁻ → AgCl; 2Ag⁺ + S²⁻ → Ag₂S; Ag⁺ + CN⁻ → AgCN
chapters.script: A silver containing precipitate is not automatically proof that an organic sample contained a halogen. In the classical converted extract model, chloride gives silver chloride, but sulfide and cyanide can also consume silver ions and form precipitates. The sulfide equation needs two silver ions per sulfide because the charges are plus one and minus two. Cyanide forms silver cyanide in a one to one ion ratio. The analytical scheme must therefore address those interferences before interpreting a silver halide result. Acid choice also matters. Hydrochloric acid introduces chloride ions itself, so it can create a false chloride signal in a silver test. A specified nitric acid treatment avoids introducing that particular halide and belongs to the controlled analytical method. This is an interpretation principle, not a prescription for acidifying an unknown extract: reactive metal residues and cyanide or sulfide species require trained laboratory supervision and suitable controls. Precipitate colour or a single reagent observation is supporting evidence rather than a unique identity. Separate the conversion step, removal of interference and detection reaction before assigning an element from the final observation.

chapters.title: Crystallization recovery differs from purity
chapters.formula: Given cold solubilities per 100 g water: A=4.0 g, B=8.0 g; sample A=10.0 g, B=2.0 g
chapters.script: Selective crystallization uses different solubilities, but high crystal purity does not require complete recovery of the desired compound. In a stipulated ideal model, a hot solution contains ten point zero grams desired solid A and two point zero grams soluble impurity B in fifty point zero grams water. On cooling, the supplied solubilities are four point zero grams A and eight point zero grams B per one hundred grams water. The liquid can retain two point zero grams A and up to four point zero grams B. Thus eight point zero grams A crystallize while all two grams B can remain dissolved. With no co crystallization or trapped liquid, the crystals are pure A in this model, but recovery is only eighty percent of the original A. A separate fresh ten gram cold water wash that reaches the stated solubility can dissolve another zero point four gram A. Remaining crystals are seven point six grams, or seventy six percent overall recovery. Real washing may not reach equilibrium, and crystal occlusion or mixed solids can affect purity. These are supplied mass balance assumptions, not guarantees of an experimental separation or a solvent handling procedure.

chapters.title: Distillation changes vapour composition
chapters.formula: Ideal liquid and ideal vapour: pi=xipi*; yA=pA/(pA+pB)
chapters.script: Distillation separates a mixture because the vapour can have a different composition from the liquid in equilibrium with it. For a supplied ideal binary liquid, let the liquid mole fraction of A be zero point two five zero and that of B zero point seven five zero. At the stated common temperature, take pure component vapour pressures one hundred kilopascals for A and forty kilopascals for B. Raoult's law gives partial pressures twenty five and thirty kilopascals, with total pressure fifty five. In an ideal vapour mixture, A therefore has mole fraction twenty five divided by fifty five, or about zero point four five five. This exceeds its liquid fraction, so the vapour is enriched in the more volatile component A. It is not pure A, and its mole fraction is not the same as its mass fraction without molar mass information. Repeated equilibration can improve separation in an appropriate fractional distillation model. Actual mixtures may be nonideal or form azeotropes, so repeated stages do not guarantee arbitrary purity for every liquid pair. State temperature, ideality and both phase compositions before interpreting a distillation question.

chapters.title: Ionization changes a weak acid’s extraction distribution
chapters.formula: D=P/(1+10^(pH−pKa)); fraction in organic phase=DVo/(Vaq+DVo) in the stated model
chapters.script: An extraction coefficient must distinguish one neutral species from all analytical forms of an acid. In a supplied supporting model, neutral H A partitions between immiscible organic and aqueous phases with coefficient P equal to ten, defined as organic neutral concentration divided by aqueous neutral concentration. Its ionized form A minus stays in water. At maintained aqueous p H and acid constant p K a four, the ratio of aqueous ionized to neutral acid is ten raised to p H minus p K a. The total analytical distribution ratio D is therefore P divided by one plus that ratio. At p H four, D is five. With one hundred millilitres aqueous phase and fifty millilitres organic phase, the equilibrium fraction of the acid inventory in organic solution is five times fifty divided by one hundred plus five times fifty, or five sevenths, about seventy one point four percent. At p H six, D drops to ten over one hundred one, and the fraction falls to about four point seven two percent. This assumes maintained p H, no organic ion transfer, no association and unchanged phase volumes; it is a specified equilibrium model, not a universal solvent preference or experimental procedure.

chapters.title: Adsorption and partition describe different retention models
chapters.formula: Normal-phase silica TLC: stronger adsorption usually means smaller Rf under matched conditions
chapters.script: Chromatography requires naming both phases and the retention mechanism, rather than treating every chromatogram as the same process. In a stipulated normal phase thin layer model, polar silica is the stationary solid and a relatively nonpolar liquid is the mobile phase. A compound that interacts more strongly with the silica spends less time moving with the solvent and can show a lower retention factor. Suppose under the same run conditions sample A travels one point two five centimetres, sample B three point seven five, and the solvent front five point zero zero. Their retention factors are zero point two five and zero point seven five. The observations are consistent with stronger retention of A in that system, not a universal molecular polarity measurement. A more strongly eluting mobile phase often competes more effectively for adsorption sites and changes both movements. In a simple partition chromatography teaching model, retention instead follows distribution between a stationary liquid and the moving phase; water associated with paper can play that stationary liquid role. Real surfaces can involve mixed interactions. State the model, solvent and stationary material before predicting a direction or transferring a ranking to another chromatographic system.

chapters.title: Sublimation separates volatility but does not certify purity
chapters.formula: Solid→vapour→solid; recovered analyte mass=collected fraction mass × assayed purity
chapters.script: Sublimation can separate a suitably volatile solid from a much less volatile impurity without requiring a stable liquid intermediate. Solid molecules enter the vapour phase and can deposit again as solid elsewhere. In an appropriate comparison, camphor is much more volatile than sodium chloride, so this property can support a separation. The method still needs adequate vapour pressure and chemical stability; a compound that decomposes is not automatically purified merely because material appears at another location. Mechanical entrainment or another volatile impurity can contaminate the collected fraction. In a supplied recovery ledger, an initial mixture contains two point zero zero grams desired solid. A collected fraction has total mass one point five zero grams and independent assay gives ninety six point zero percent desired compound. Recovered analyte is one point four four grams, giving seventy two point zero percent recovery. Dividing one point five zero directly by two point zero zero would give seventy five percent, but would count impurity as product. Purity describes the composition of the collected fraction; recovery describes the desired amount retained from the original inventory. This is interpretation of phase behaviour and assay data, not an apparatus or heating procedure.

chapters.script: Selective crystallization requires following the desired substance and the impurity separately. Use a supplied ideal model with ten grams of A and two grams of B in fifty grams of water. Hot solubilities are twenty grams A and ten grams B per hundred grams of water, allowing all of both substances to dissolve. At the specified cold temperature, solubilities become two grams A and six grams B per hundred grams of water. The cold mother liquor can therefore retain one gram A and up to three grams B. Nine grams A crystallize, while all two grams B can remain dissolved. This assumes independent solubilities, unchanged solvent mass and no mixed crystals or trapped mother liquor. Now stipulate a separate equilibrium wash of the isolated crystals with ten grams of fresh water at that same cold temperature. Its capacity for A is two tenths of a gram, leaving eight point eight grams A if that dissolution loss is reached. Recovery of A is then eighty eight percent of its original ten grams. A solubility ledger predicts ideal separation and loss; it does not experimentally certify purity when occlusion, adsorption or nonideal mixed solution effects occur.

At fifty kilopascals it is one hundred degrees, and at one hundred kilopascals it is one hundred thirty. Lowering pressure allows boiling at a lower temperature because the vapour pressure needs to match a smaller external pressure. It does not change molecular identity or prove that decomposition and bumping cannot occur. Use absolute pressure rather than inserting an unconverted gauge reading. The numerical table concerns a pure component; a mixture needs its own phase equilibrium information. chapters.title: Supporting chromatography: retention and resolution answer different questions
chapters.formula: k=(tR−tM)/tM; Rs=2(tR,B−tR,A)/(wA+wB) for supplied baseline widths
chapters.script: A chromatographic retention time includes the time taken by material that is not retained. In a supporting column model, let the measured dead time be one minute and the two retention times four and five minutes. The retention factor for a peak is its adjusted retention time divided by dead time, giving three for A and four for B. The selectivity ratio using those adjusted factors is four thirds, not five fourths from the raw retention times. Separation quality also depends on peak widths. Define resolution here as twice the difference of retention times divided by the sum of the two baseline widths. If both supplied baseline widths are half a minute, resolution is two. If both broaden to one point two minutes while their retention times stay fixed, resolution falls to about zero point eight three three. Distinct peak centres alone therefore do not guarantee well resolved components. The width convention must remain explicit because a half height formula uses a different numerical coefficient. These supporting quantities describe the supplied chromatogram and do not establish molecular identity or purity from a single retention value.

chapters.title: Nitrogen estimation needs quantitative conversion as well as a nitrogen atom
chapters.formula: Dumas: n(N atoms)=2n(N2); ordinary Kjeldahl excludes nitro, azo and selected ring nitrogen
chapters.script: A nitrogen percentage is reliable only when the method converts the relevant nitrogen quantitatively into its measured form. A molecular formula containing nitrogen does not guarantee that every estimation method will recover it. In the elementary Dumas model, nitrogen is ultimately measured as molecular nitrogen after other gaseous products and interfering nitrogen oxides have been dealt with. One mole of nitrogen gas represents two moles of nitrogen atoms. For a supplied dry, corrected gas amount of zero point zero zero two mole from a zero point four zero zero gram sample, the nitrogen mass is zero point zero five six gram, giving fourteen percent. The ordinary textbook Kjeldahl method follows a different conversion. Nitrogen is first converted into ammonium ions. The stated analytical balance then liberates and captures ammonia gas to provide the measured amount. Nitro nitrogen, azo nitrogen and nitrogen in a ring such as pyridine are standard limitations of that unmodified method. A modified analytical method may extend the scope, but its recovery must be established separately. A small ammonia result for an unsuitable sample is not proof that nitrogen is absent. Always state the conversion chemistry and the measured nitrogen species before calculating a percentage.

chapters.title: Combined nitrogen and sulfur can give thiocyanate rather than separate cyanide evidence
chapters.formula: Selected fusion map: Na+C+N+S→NaSCN; Fe3++SCN−⇌[FeSCN]2+
chapters.script: Element detection depends on what species the analytical conversion actually produces. In the usual simplified sodium fusion picture, carbon and nitrogen can give cyanide, while sulfur can give sulfide. When nitrogen and sulfur are both present, a selected pathway produces thiocyanate instead. Thiocyanate can form a red iron three complex, represented in a simple equilibrium as iron three plus thiocyanate giving iron thiocyanate two plus. The charge changes from a total of plus two on the left to plus two on the right. This is a coordination equilibrium, not a requirement that the iron change oxidation state. If nitrogen has entered thiocyanate rather than free cyanide, expecting an ordinary cyanide based blue test without considering conversion conditions can lead to a false negative. The actual fusion products depend on conditions, and excess sodium can change the simplified product map. The red colour is evidence within a controlled analytical context, not a unique proof that an unknown originally contained both elements. External thiocyanate or other coloured species can interfere. Compare blanks and independent evidence before identifying the original compound. These are reaction principles rather than laboratory instructions.

chapters.title: A halide test must remove competing silver precipitates without adding the analyte
chapters.formula: Ag++Cl−→AgCl; Ag++CN−→AgCN; 2Ag++S2−→Ag2S
chapters.script: A precipitate formed with silver ions is not automatically a silver halide. A sodium fusion extract may contain cyanide or sulfide, and these species can also consume silver ions to form sparingly soluble products. The simplified equations use one silver ion per cyanide and two silver ions per sulfide. In a supplied bookkeeping example, zero point zero zero one mole of cyanide and the same amount of sulfide could consume zero point zero zero three mole of silver ions even if no halide were present. The textbook analytical logic therefore requires removal or destruction of the interfering species before interpreting a halide precipitation result. Acid choice is part of the blank: adding hydrochloric acid would introduce chloride and could create the very result being sought. Nitric acid is used in the conventional conceptual scheme because it does not introduce a halide. Merely lowering the pH does not prove that all interfering species have been removed quantitatively. Their conversion and absence must be established. This discussion explains selectivity and contamination; it is not a procedure for generating or handling the hazardous gases associated with these methods.

quiz.question: Why is hydrochloric acid unsuitable as an uncontaminated acid blank before testing an extract for chloride?
options: It introduces the chloride being tested for
quiz.explanation: Hydrochloric acid adds chloride, which can form AgCl independently of chloride originally present in the sample.

quiz.question: In the stated direct oxygen model, .001 mol I2 corresponds to how many moles of sample O atoms?
quiz.explanation: The balanced I2O5+5CO reaction maps five sample oxygen atoms in CO to each iodine molecule.

quiz.question: The stated .400 g sample gives .254 g I2, with M(I2)=254 and O=16. Its oxygen percentage is:
quiz.explanation: The iodine amount is .001 mol, so sample oxygen is 5×.001×16=.080 g and .080/.400×100=20%.
